content: Xylene refers to a group of three chemical compounds that are isomers of dimethylbenzene: ortho-xylene, meta-xylene, and para-xylene. These isomers differ based on the positions of the two methyl groups attached to the benzene ring. In ortho-xylene (o-xylene), the methyl groups are attached to adjacent carbon atoms, and its IUPAC name is 1,2-dimethylbenzene. In meta-xylene (m-xylene), the methyl groups are separated by one carbon atom, and its IUPAC name is 1,3-dimethylbenzene. In para-xylene (p-xylene), the methyl groups are located opposite each other on the benzene ring, and its IUPAC name is 1,4-dimethylbenzene. Xylene is a colorless liquid with a sweet odor and is highly flammable. It occurs naturally in substances like petroleum and coal tar and can also be produced during forest fires. The physical properties of xylene vary slightly depending on the isomer. For example, the melting points range from −47.87°C (−54.17°F) for m-xylene to 13.26°C (55.87°F) for p-xylene. The boiling points of all isomers are approximately 140°C (284°F). Xylene has a density of about 0.87 kg/L, making it less dense than water. In air, xylene can be detected by smell at concentrations as low as 0.08 to 3.7 parts per million (ppm), and it can be tasted in water at concentrations between 0.53 and 1.8 ppm. Industrially, xylene is produced from petroleum and is one of the most widely manufactured chemicals in the United States. It is used as a solvent in various industries, including printing, rubber, and leather manufacturing. Para-xylene (p-xylene) is particularly important as a precursor in the production of terephthalic acid, which is a key component in the manufacture of polymers. Xylene is also used as a cleaning agent for steel, silicon wafers, and chips, as well as a pesticide, a paint thinner, and an ingredient in paints and varnishes. It can replace toluene in lacquers when slower drying is desired. Additionally, xylene is present in small amounts in aviation fuel and gasoline. In laboratory settings, xylene is sometimes applied to the ears of rabbits to enhance blood flow for collection, but the area must be cleaned with alcohol afterward to prevent inflammation. Xylene serves as a precursor for the synthesis of other chemicals. For example, chlorination of xylene produces xylylene dichlorides, also known as 1,2-bis(chloromethyl)benzene, which can exist in three isomeric forms. When oxidized with agents like potassium permanganate (KMnO4), the methyl groups in xylene can be converted into carboxylic acid groups. Oxidation of both methyl groups in o-xylene results in phthalic acid, while oxidation of p-xylene yields terephthalic acid. These concentrations can also harm the mothers. People exposed to contaminated soil or groundwater may experience adverse health effects, especially if the groundwater is used as a drinking water source.
